issues.description: Trainer complects DeepSpeed engine, wandb logging, checkpoint discovery, dtype derivation, and reduction in one class
issues.detail: DeepSpeedTrainer braids together five separable concerns: engine init, wandb side effects, filesystem checkpoint scanning, dtype inference from config, and all_reduce. None of these need to know about the others. Pull each into a pure function over data (config dict in, value out) and a thin orchestrator. The class is COMPLECTED.

issues.description: Module-level wandb is a hidden global identity masquerading as a value sink
issues.detail: wandb.log/wandb.config.update are place-oriented calls to an implicit singleton initialized in train.py and asserted (by docstring, not code) in the trainer. The trainer's behavior depends on a global mutable place established elsewhere. Pass a logger object (or a no-op logger on non-zero ranks) explicitly; the value flow becomes visible and testable. PLACE-ORIENTED.

issues.description: Data specifier strings are stringly-typed values that should be parsed data
issues.detail: 'task:name:data_json[:factor]' is a value pretending to be a string. It is split with .split() in train.py and re-parsed downstream. Parse once at the edge into a small dataclass or dict {task, name, path, factor}; pass the value, not the encoding. Right now the same parsing logic must exist in multiple places. EASY-NOT-SIMPLE.

issues.description: _load_checkpoint conflates 'where the checkpoint is' with 'what step we are at'
issues.detail: Checkpoint discovery parses the step number out of a directory name (split('step_')[-1]) and also reads global_step from client_state, then trusts client_state. Two sources of truth for the same fact. Make the directory name a hint for ordering only; the step is a value stored inside the checkpoint. Today a renamed directory silently changes which checkpoint wins.

issues.description: run() calls valid() and save_checkpoint after every train() block with no condition
issues.detail: The loop runs train() for save_interval steps, then unconditionally validates and checkpoints. val_interval is documented but never read. save_interval is the only knob, and it drives three different time semantics (training chunk size, validation cadence, checkpoint cadence) at once. Three identities, one number. Separate them.

issues.description: train_dtype reads config repeatedly instead of treating the config as a value once
issues.detail: ds_config.get('bf16', {}).get('enabled', False) chains repeat across three branches. A small pure function precision_from_config(ds_config) -> torch.dtype is clearer and trivially testable without DeepSpeed. Minor, but illustrative of the broader pattern: data is in your hands; transform it, don't poke at it.

review.summary: The functionality is reasonable but the trainer class is a classic case of complecting: engine, logging, checkpoint discovery, dtype, and reduction all live in one place, and the value flow runs through a global wandb singleton instead of an explicit logger argument. Stringly-typed specifiers and a save_interval that secretly controls three different cadences are the most visible symptoms. The fix is not more abstraction; it is fewer concerns per object and more values passed explicitly. The question that should have been asked first: what are the values (config, checkpoint, batch stats), what are the identities (model_engine, global_step, logger), and what is the time model (train cadence vs. valid cadence vs. save cadence) — and are they the same thing or three things wearing one name?
